sections.overview: The cerulean kingfisher is a very small member of the kingfisher family, Alcedinidae. Its natural range is restricted to Indonesia, including southern Sumatra, Java, Bali and islands east toward Flores.
sections.identification: It is a tiny, compact kingfisher with bright blue to turquoise upperparts, a narrow blue breast band, and white throat, face patches and underparts. The dark bill is long and pointed; the legs are reddish brown. Adults measure about 13–14 cm and weigh around 35 g; these references give no standard wingspan, body height or width. Males are usually bluer, while females have a greener cast and a narrower breast band; juveniles are duller, greyish and may lack a clear band. These contrasts help separate it from the dark, blue-eared kingfisher and from larger, white-and-orange common kingfishers.
sections.habitat: It lives beside coastal marshes, mangroves, estuaries, small streams, canals, ponds and fishponds, using both fresh and brackish water. Records extend from southern Sumatra and Java through Bali and the Lesser Sunda Islands, with local reports reaching Flores.
sections.diet: It takes small fish, aquatic insects and crustaceans. It watches from a waterside perch and plunges for prey; over open water it may hover briefly before diving.
sections.behavior: The bird often sits on low branches or posts beside water, then dives rapidly after prey. Field observations from Java also describe short hovering dives, sometimes from about 2–4 m above the water; this is a locally documented hunting technique, not a claim that it hovers constantly.
sections.reproduction: In Java, breeding has been recorded in April–June, August and October, so the available records do not indicate one short, island-wide season. The pair excavates a sloping tunnel in an earthen bank; reported clutches contain three to six white eggs.
sections.ecology: Field observations on Java’s north coast found it hunting from perches around mangrove creeks, mudflats and fishponds, then hovering briefly and diving for aquatic prey.
sections.conservation: The Indonesian biodiversity record lists the species as Least Concern, and an Indonesian fauna guide quotes a 2019 summary as Least Concern with a stable trend. This is a dated broad assessment and does not establish the trend of every local wetland population.
